summary: The note surveys eco-art, the movement in which artists use their work to address environmental crises, tracing it from its late 20th-century roots to current practitioners. It profiles artists and projects spanning installation, activism, conservation and education, and argues that eco-artists will play a growing role in shaping public opinion and policy, including through digital and virtual reality tools.
one_line: An overview of eco-art, profiling artists and projects that use creative work to advance environmental awareness, activism, conservation and education.
key_facts: Eco-art emerged as a defined movement in the late 20th century, when artists began challenging the idea that art should be only for art's sake.
Betty Beaumont created "Ocean Landmark" in 1975, transforming 500 tons of processed coal waste into a thriving marine environment.
Maya Lin, known for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C., created the multimedia project "What is Missing?" about the loss of biodiversity.
Olafur Eliasson's "Ice Watch" series confronts viewers with the physicality of melting icebergs to represent the threat of climate change.

Lily Kim makes installations from recycled industrial materials and live plants; her piece "Breathable Cities" critiques unsustainable urban development, and she drew public attention on October 15, 2023.
Emily Carr's "Urban Rewilding" series began on November 9, 2023, with collaborative performances planting native species in concrete-dominated neighborhoods.
Tomás Saraceno collaborates with scientists, engineers, and arachnologists; his "Aerocene" project consists of airborne sculptures that float without burning fossil fuels.
Anna O'Hara's "Seed Paper Portraits," begun in 2024, use biodegradable paper infused with native plant seeds that germinate when planted.
The collective "The Green Brushes" began the project "Reverence Revealed" on September 5, 2023, painting murals with air-cleaning paint on buildings in polluted cities.
Aaron Li launched "EcoLabs" on September 22, 2023, bringing together artists, scientists, and community members to create site-specific art that educates about ecology.
The note says virtual reality, digital platforms, and interactive experiences offer eco-artists new ways to reach global audiences.
